{{Short description|Dimensionless measure in cosmology}}
{{More citations needed|date=February 2011}}
{{Cosmology}}
The '''deceleration parameter <math>q</math>''' in cosmology is a [[dimensionless]] measure of the [[Accelerating expansion of the universe|cosmic acceleration]] of the [[expansion of space]] in a [[Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric|Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker universe]].  It is defined by:
<math display="block">q \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\  -\frac{\ddot{a} a }{\dot{a}^2}</math>
where <math>a</math> is the [[Scale factor (cosmology)|scale factor of the universe]] and the dots indicate derivatives by [[proper time]]. The expansion of the universe is said to be "accelerating" if <math>\ddot{a} > 0</math> (recent measurements suggest it is), and in this case the deceleration parameter will be negative.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Mark H. |last2=Lambourne  |first2=Robert J. |title=An Introduction to Galaxies and Cosmology |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |date=2004 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=36K1PfetZegC&pg=PA244|page=244|isbn=978-0-521-83738-5}}</ref> The minus sign and name "deceleration parameter" are historical; at the time of definition <math>\ddot{a}</math> was expected to be negative, so a minus sign was inserted in the definition to make <math>q</math> positive in that case. Since the evidence for the [[accelerating universe]] in the 1998–2003 era, it is now believed that <math>\ddot{a}</math> is positive therefore the present-day value <math>q_0</math> is negative (though <math> q </math> was positive in the past before dark energy became dominant). In general <math> q </math> varies with cosmic time, except in a few special cosmological models; the present-day value is denoted <math>q_0</math>. 

The [[Friedmann equations|Friedmann acceleration equation]] can be written as
<math display="block">\frac{\ddot{a}}{a} =-\frac{4 \pi G}{3} \sum_i (\rho_i +\frac{3\,p_i}{c^2})= -\frac{4\pi G}{3} \sum_i \rho_i (1 + 3 w_i), </math>
where the sum <math>i</math> extends over the different components, matter, radiation and dark energy, <math>\rho_i</math> is the equivalent mass density of each component, <math>p_i</math> is its pressure, and <math>w_i = p_i/(\rho_i c^2) </math> is the [[Equation of state (cosmology)|equation of state]] for each component. The value of <math>w_i</math> is 0 for non-relativistic matter (baryons and dark matter), 1/3 for radiation, and −1 for a [[cosmological constant]]; for more general [[dark energy]] it may differ from −1, in which case it is denoted <math>w_{DE}</math> or simply <math> w </math>.

Defining the critical density as
<math display="block"> \rho_{c} = \frac{3 H^2}{8 \pi G} </math> 
and the density parameters <math> \Omega_i \equiv \rho_i / \rho_c </math>, substituting <math>\rho_i = \Omega_i\,\rho_c</math> in the acceleration equation gives
<math display="block">q= \frac{1}{2} \sum \Omega_i (1+3w_i) = \Omega_\text{rad}(z) +\frac{1}{2}\Omega_m(z) + \frac{1+3w_\text{DE} }{2} \Omega_\text{DE}(z) \ . </math>
where the density parameters are at the relevant cosmic epoch.  
At the present day <math> \Omega_\text{rad} \sim 10^{-4} </math> is negligible, and if <math> w_{DE} = -1 </math> (cosmological constant) this simplifies to 
<math display="block"> q_0 = \frac{1}{2} \Omega_m - \Omega_\Lambda . </math> 
where the density parameters are present-day values; with Ω<sub>Λ</sub> + Ω<sub>m</sub> ≈ 1, and Ω<sub>Λ</sub> = 0.7 and then Ω<sub>m</sub> = 0.3, this evaluates to <math> q_0 \approx -0.55 </math> for the parameters estimated from the [[Planck spacecraft]] data.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Camarena |first1=David |last2=Marra |first2=Valerio |date=January 2020 |title=Local determination of the Hubble constant and the deceleration parameter |journal = Physical Review Research |volume=2 |issue=1 |article-number=013028 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.2.013028|arxiv=1906.11814 |bibcode=2020PhRvR...2a3028C |doi-access=free }}</ref> (Note that the CMB, as a high-redshift measurement, does not directly measure <math>q_0</math>; but its value can be inferred by fitting cosmological models to the CMB data, then calculating <math>q_0</math> from the other measured parameters as above).

The time derivative of the [[Hubble parameter]] can be written in terms of the deceleration parameter:
<math display="block">\frac{\dot{H}}{H^2}=-(1+q).</math>

Except in the speculative case of [[phantom energy]] (which violates all the energy conditions), all postulated forms of mass-energy yield a deceleration parameter <math>q \geqslant -1.</math> Thus, any non-phantom universe should have a decreasing Hubble parameter, except in the case of the distant future of a [[Lambda-CDM model]], where <math>q</math> will tend to −1 from above and the Hubble parameter will asymptote to a constant value of <math> H_0 \sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda} </math>.

The above results imply that the universe would be decelerating for any cosmic fluid with equation of state <math>w</math> greater than <math>-\tfrac{1}{3}</math> (any fluid satisfying the [[strong energy condition]] does so, as does any form of matter present in the [[Standard Model]], but excluding inflation). However observations of distant [[type Ia supernova]]e indicate that <math>q</math> is negative; the expansion of the universe is accelerating.  This is an indication that the gravitational attraction of matter, on the cosmological scale, is more than counteracted by the negative pressure of [[dark energy]], in the form of either [[Quintessence (physics)|quintessence]] or a positive [[cosmological constant]].

Before the first indications of an accelerating universe, in 1998, it was thought that the universe was dominated by matter with negligible pressure, <math>w \approx 0.</math> This implied that the deceleration parameter would be equal to <math> \Omega_m/2 </math>, e.g. <math> q_0 = 1/2 </math> for a universe with <math> \Omega_m = 1 </math> or <math> q_0 \sim 0.1 </math> for a low-density zero-Lambda model. The experimental effort to discriminate these cases with supernovae actually revealed negative <math> q_0 \sim -0.6 \pm 0.2 </math>, evidence for cosmic acceleration, which has subsequently grown stronger.
